issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are strongly social-evaluative and interpersonal (avoiding evaluation, avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which contains no social threat, shame, or interpersonal trauma content to explain these strategies.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, the strongest pathway is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies. However, the selected negative appraisals focus on global identity change, chronic misery, and self-blame for being in the situation, while the selected strategies are specifically about managing social scrutiny and interpersonal interactions. That is a weak clinical fit: the strategies do not plausibly follow from the appraisals provided.

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Memory and appraisals are only partly coherent: terror on recall and olfactory recall fit disaster trauma, but rage on recall is less well supported by the rest of the profile because there is no accompanying appraisal about betrayal, preventability by others, or injustice that would explain intense anger as a central recall response.

For a natural-disaster trauma, intense rage specifically on recall is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on terror, misery, self-change, and generalized avoidance rather than anger at a person or agent. Rage can occur, but here it lacks support from the other selected items and is the least coherent memory item.

'Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation' implies preventable personal failure in getting into the trauma. With a natural disaster, this appraisal is difficult to justify unless there was a very specific risky decision context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The other appraisals focus on post-trauma change and unhappiness, making this item the clearest mismatch.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, strong self-blame framed as 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to justify clinically unless the disaster involved a very specific preventable action by the patient. In the absence of any such context, this appraisal is implausible for the indexed trauma.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are predominantly interpersonal/social-safety behaviors (avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations) that fit social threat or shame-based trauma formulations more than a natural disaster PTSD presentation. They do not connect well to the memory/appraisal content provided.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile includes active hypervigilant threat-monitoring ('constantly scan environment for signs of threat') and a global danger appraisal, but the formulation specifies Threat as effectively inactive, with no active links involving Threat and no active Trigger pathways. For a natural-disaster case, these items imply an ongoing threat-focused maintenance pattern that is not supported by the stated formulation.

issues.item: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
issues.explanation: This is not just a weak-edge issue: both items explicitly center current external danger/threat, whereas the active formulation is concentrated on Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory and Negative Appraisals ↔ Maladaptive Strategies without Threat involvement. The remaining items fit a self-focused/post-traumatic change formulation, making these threat-focused items the main incoherent elements.

vignette:
Marcus

Marcus was nineteen when the tornado came through his hometown near Springfield, Illinois, on a March evening in 2023. He had been working his shift at the McDonald's on Route 66 when the manager told everyone to get away from the windows. Marcus remembered the sound first-not the wind itself but the roar beneath it, something alive and hungry. He remembered the smell of ozone and wet soil pouring through the ventilation system. The building shook. A customer screamed. Then, in the chaos of the evacuation, Marcus found himself separated from the group, pressed into a storage closet with two other employees, listening to what sounded like the world tearing apart outside. When the noise stopped and they emerged, the parking lot was unrecognizable-cars overturned, debris everywhere, a utility pole snapped like kindling. Marcus had walked away physically unharmed, but something in him had fractured in that closet.

In the months that followed, Marcus noticed changes he couldn't quite name. The vividness of his memories disturbed him most. When he tried to recall the event-and he found himself trying constantly, as though understanding it better might make it less real-the images came back sharp and complete. He could see the fluorescent lights flickering, the crack spreading across the ceiling tile, the faces of his coworkers frozen in fear. Worse was the sensory intrusion: when these images surfaced, often unbidden, he could smell the ozone again, could taste the dust that had settled on his tongue. The terror came back too, not as a thought but as a physical sensation, his chest tightening, his breath shortening, his body convinced it was happening again.

Marcus had started rehearsing conversations weeks before his first therapy appointment. Before his shift, he would stand in his bedroom and whisper through interactions with customers, managers, other employees-scripting every word, every inflection, terrified that if he wasn't prepared, something would go wrong. At work, he'd arrive early to mentally map the building, identifying exits, calculating distances, checking weather forecasts obsessively. His manager had noticed him becoming withdrawn and unreliable. Twice he'd called in sick when the forecast mentioned thunderstorms. Once, when a customer raised their voice about a wrong order, Marcus had felt his body flood with panic and had to step into the back room to breathe.

Beyond the rehearsal and avoidance, Marcus had begun trying to suppress the memories themselves. When an image surfaced-the crack in the ceiling, the smell of ozone-he would shake his head hard, as though he could physically dislodge it, or he would turn up music, scroll through his phone, do anything to interrupt the thought. But the memories kept returning, more insistent each time he tried to push them away.

What troubled Marcus most, though, was not the memories or the panic but the person he had become in their wake. He used to be someone who joked around at work, who made plans with friends on weekends, who felt generally okay about his life. Now he was someone who couldn't leave his house without a script, who cancelled plans because the idea of being anywhere unpredictable made his stomach turn, who felt a constant, grinding misery that had become so familiar it seemed permanent. He had come to believe that the tornado hadn't just passed through his town-it had passed through him, and what remained was damaged in a way that couldn't be repaired. His friends had tried to reach out, but he'd withdrawn from them. His parents worried. He worried most of all.

Marcus finally made an appointment after his manager pulled him aside and said his performance was suffering, that he needed to "get help or find another job." Sitting in the waiting room, Marcus felt the familiar knot of dread. He was certain that talking about it would only make the memories sharper, the terror more real. But he was also certain that he couldn't keep living like this-rehearsing, avoiding, suppressing, drowning in the person he'd become. He needed to know if the person he used to be was still somewhere inside, or if the tornado had taken that too.
